items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Al and I started rehearsing with Mary Lou Williams... After a few rehearsals with Mary Lou, we recorded for a small company called Asch records.

ctx.x: I was in St. Louis on Sunday the 7th of December, 1941, when an extra edition of newspapers came out with the news that the Japanese had bombarded Pearl Harbour, but I really got the news from Al Sears who came to my room in the Booker Washington Hotel and told me that he was going to have his family leave New York because he though the Japanese may bombard the Apple next.

During the week, Harold Baker, who was Mary Lou's ole man, had a dispute with Mary and gave Andy his notice and said that he was going to stay in St. Louis. I think that he had over accepted to work with some orchestra. So Andy had contacted his booking agency which was Joe Glaser, the one that booked Armstrong also, and asked Joe to send him a trumpet player to replace Harold. Two days before we closed, a trumpet player named Howard McGhee arrived. Andy called a rehearsal for the next afternoon and when I…

Then arrived the day for us to leave St. Louis and Harold "Shorty Boo" Baker had changed his mind and couldn't stand to let his sweet Mary Lou leave him, and it seems as though Mary Lou may have left the band if Andy hadn't agreed to take Shorty back. Andy didn't want to lose Mary Lou, so he was stuck with four trumpeters because McGhee had been sent to him by Glaser and he was obliged to keep him.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Al and I started rehearsing with Mary Lou Williams who had enjoyed the way we sounded when she replaced Ellis at the Cafe Society Uptown.

ctx.x: There were only three musicians in the orchestra that I knew slightly and they were Harold Baker, trumpet, whom I had seen with Teddy Wilson's big band, Henry Wells, trombone, in Lunceford's orchestra and Edward Inge, ex-Don Redman clarinetist. The rest of the member were Harry Lawson, known as "Big Jim", Ted Donnelly, trombone, Johnny Harrington and Buddy Miller, alto-sax's, Dick Wilson, tenor. Floyd Smith, guitar, Booker Collins, bass, Mary Lou Williams, piano, Ben Thigpen, drums and June Richmond, vocals.

I had however seen Andy Kirk and his "Clouds of Joy" quite a few times when he had a male singer named Pha Terrell with him and had also admired the piano playing of Mary Lou Williams who played strong swinging piano like a man. I soon found out that Mary Lou was a fine arranger also because there were quite a number of compositions in the Kirk book that were written and arranged by her and they were swinging stomping arrangements.

items.title: 53571_Mary Lou Williams oral history interview
items.q: I had taken Bill Coleman and Al Hail with me

ctx.x: I don't know what happened because see I was working on the East Side and various places out of the city, but when I got this job I was alternating with Billy Taylor. I can't remember the name of this place, at 52nd and Eighth Avenue. So I had a way of always helping musicians. At one time I was recording for Moe Asch and what happened, he was expecting a pianist and I had taken Bill Coleman and Al Hail with me and he got a little peeved about it but he recorded it, because they were out of work and I put them…
